cloud.failure_mode: Nothing breaks, because there is nothing to break: the app contains no HTTP client, endpoint, account system, cloud sync or OTA mechanism at all (checked across the whole app; the manifest's INTERNET permission is unused by app code). The only vendor-disappearance risk is the app being delisted from the store — and everything the app does is reproducible from this spec.
cloud.notes: Recorded explicitly because a spec with no cloud block could read as 'cloud not yet investigated'. Here the ABSENCE is the verified finding. Sharing between users is done out-of-band (the admin password is sent as an SMS), not via any server.
cloud.vendor_service: None — no cloud service exists for this product

identity.notes: The app keys locks by their MAC address. The one captured unit uses a public address (OUI F4:04:4C, Valence) that stayed constant across sessions; whether the whole family is public-addressed is unknown — if a unit turns out to rotate its address, key on the manufacturer-data status byte stream instead and re-resolve the address by scanning.

manufacturer_data.description:
The lock broadcasts manufacturer-specific data whose first entry's payload is a single status byte, with the same layout as the notify status byte (see the 67ac8801 characteristic's `status_byte` field). A passive observer can therefore track lock state and battery without ever connecting.
The Bluetooth SIG company ID in the header is NOT recoverable from the app code (it reads the first SparseArray key, whatever it is), and the 2026-08-30 capture contains no advertising reports, so the company ID and the exact AD structure around the status byte are still unconfirmed — do not filter on company ID until one is observed. For reference, the vendor app scans unfiltered, with a 2 s batch report delay inside a 10 s window.

device.manufacturer: BIO-key International, Inc. (locks built on a shared OEM platform; the companion app is published by a third-party developer)
device.name: BIO-key TouchLock BT family
device.notes:
Family of Bluetooth Low Energy fingerprint/keyless locks sold under the BIO-key TouchLock BT brand (launched CES 2017 per BIO-key SEC filings). The TouchLock consumer hardware line appears discontinued — the product pages are gone from bio-key.com — but BIO-key International itself is still in business. FCC ID 2AIKJ-BL (grantee BIO-KEY) covers the padlock models BL0509/BL1209/BS1609. TouchLock variants that carry a fingerprint sensor but no BLE exist and are NOT covered here.
The Android app's package name points at the ODM rather than at BIO-key, and the app recognizes advertised names that BIO-key never shipped (Joi_Lock), so this spec covers a shared OEM protocol across a family of rebadged locks, not only BIO-key-branded ones. Non-BIO-key siblings are assumed to speak the identical protocol because the same app drives them — that assumption is unverified (no capture of an OEM sibling exists).
The most useful fact about this family: it has NO cloud at all. The app requests INTERNET permission but a sweep of the whole app finds no HTTP client, endpoint, account system, sync or OTA mechanism (the settings screen's upgrade row is unconditionally hidden and the upgrade event class is empty). The lock cannot die from a cloud shutdown.
Security assessment: there is no real cryptography. The rolling credential is the current timestamp yy-MM-dd-HH-mm-ss-SSSS split into eight two-digit decimal groups, each written as one byte parsed as hex. Protection rests on BLE bonding plus this obfuscation; anyone who observes one exchange and knows the approximate time can replay or predict credentials. For a local integration this is a convenience — a client can generate valid commands with no secrets beyond enrollment — but nobody should treat the lock's electronic path as high-security.

exclusivity.recovery: Disconnect the vendor app before connecting. Because the app drops its bond on every disconnect, a stale bond is not usually what is in the way — an open session is.

pairing.notes: Capture-confirmed (2026-08-30): bonding is enforced and there is no PIN. The lock's first L2CAP packet after connect is an SMP security request; pairing is legacy Just Works (the lock's IO capability is NoInputNoOutput), bonding flags are set, and LTK/IRK/CSRK are distributed in both directions. ATT service discovery only happens after pairing completes — a central that never bonds (the failure seen with an unpairing client) discovers zero services and the lock drops the link. Error code 0x07 (unbonded device) is the protocol-level refusal that matches. Treat the bond as the only real barrier, and a weak one: the password scheme is predictable to anyone who has watched one exchange and knows roughly what time it is.

unpair.clears: The transient bond only; enrolled fingerprints and admin records survive.
unpair.notes: The vendor app deliberately unpairs on disconnect on Android 7+, so bonds here are transient by design rather than persistent state somebody has to manage. A client that assumes a durable bond will find one is not there next time.

security_advisory.detail: There is no real cryptography. The rolling "password" is the current timestamp (yy-MM-dd-HH-mm-ss-SSSS) split into eight two-digit decimal groups, each parsed as a single hex byte, and the previous value is kept as a one-shot fallback. Because it is derived entirely from the clock it is predictable to anyone who knows the approximate time and trivially replayable to anyone who captures a single legitimate unlock. The only barrier is BLE Just Works bonding (no PIN), which the companion app itself drops on every disconnect. Affected: the whole TouchLock BT family and the OEM rebadges that speak the same protocol. This assessment is derived from static analysis of the companion app (see `evidence`); it has not been replayed against hardware and no over-the-air capture exists, so it is reported rather than demonstrated.
security_advisory.summary: The unlock credential is a predictable, replayable time-derived value — anyone who observes one exchange, or just knows the approximate time, can replay or forge unlock commands; only weak Just Works bonding stands in the way.

issued_to_client: None device-generated — the client INVENTS the admin ID and password at enrollment and must store them
credentials.notes: No WiFi exists anywhere in the product. All credentials are client-generated and pushed to the lock; losing the client's stored credentials means re-enrolling via factory reset.
stored_on_device: Admin ID (8 bytes) and current rolling time-based password
Enrolled user records (user IDs + their passwords)
Factory password (8 characters, default hinted as 00000000)
Lock RTC (synced by the client before every unlock)

factory_reset.effect: FactoryInit (0x8f) returns the lock to the unregistered state, clearing the admin ID, all enrolled users and the rolling password; every client must re-enroll afterwards. No physical reset procedure is documented in the app — reset is a BLE command, gated by the factory password. Confidence low: the reset itself was never sent in the capture (only the factory-PASSWORD change, 0x8c/0x8d, was), and on a lock a botched reset flow can leave the owner locked out.

steps.action: Connect, bond, enable notifications as in enrollment.
Send FactoryInit (0x8f): payload A = the 8-byte admin ID, payload B = the 8-character factory password, one hex-digit character per byte.
steps.expect: Notify response: opcode echo 8f, error code 00; the lock returns to the unregistered state.
steps.notes: The app's own dialog hints the default factory password is 00000000 (eight zero characters -> bytes 0x00 x8). A changed factory password can only be replaced via ChangeFactoryPasswordRequest (0x8c) + ChangeFactoryInitPasswordData (0x8d) while the old one is known — that pair is observed in the capture, with the 0x8d frame carrying the old password as eight 0x00 bytes. If both the admin credentials and a changed factory password are lost, no software recovery path is known.

ble.pin_source: No PIN — the capture confirms legacy Just Works pairing: the lock's first packet after connect is an SMP security request, its IO capability is NoInputNoOutput, bonding flags are set, and LTK/IRK/CSRK are distributed both ways. No GATT service discovery completes before the bond exists. Note the vendor app deliberately UNPAIRS on disconnect (Android 7+), so bonds are transient in the official flow.

methods.description: Admin enrollment over GATT: bond, enable notifications, then send RegisterAdmin with a fresh time-derived admin ID and password. Entirely lock<->client; no server is involved at any point. Observed end-to-end in the 2026-08-30 capture (verified: false stays — that flag is for a flow executed from THIS spec).

steps.action: Scan unfiltered; select candidates by advertised name pattern and the presence of a manufacturer-data status byte.
Connect and bond (Just Works, no PIN). The lock initiates security immediately on connect and refuses commands from unbonded centrals with error 0x07.
Discover services and enable notifications on 67ac8801-a0eb-11e6-80f5-76304dec7eb7 (CCCD 0x2902).
steps.expect: The app waits ~1.2 s after service discovery before sending its first command; mirror that delay. Once notifications are on, the lock pushes an unsolicited UpdateStatus (0xff) frame about once per second for the whole connection.

steps.action: If the lock is factory-fresh it accepts RegisterAdmin; an already-enrolled lock answers error 05 (already registered). Do not gate this on the advertised status byte — which bit pattern marks 'unregistered' is unconfirmed.

Send RegisterAdmin (0x80): payload A = fresh 8-byte admin ID (the app derives it from the current time, colon-joined hex), payload B = current time-based password (see `protocol_details.command_protocol.crypto`).
steps.expect: Notify response: opcode echo 80, error code 00 (success) — observed in the capture.

steps.action: Cache the admin ID and current password locally — they are the only credentials, and there is no recovery path other than factory reset.

setup.notes: No network provisioning exists (there is no radio but BLE), but the lock must be ENROLLED before it will open: an unregistered lock accepts RegisterAdmin (0x80), which installs an 8-byte admin ID and the first time-based password. The full enrollment exchange — bond, notifications on, RegisterAdmin, success response — is observed in the 2026-08-30 capture, hence high confidence; it has not yet been run by a third-party client. Which status-byte pattern advertises the unregistered state is unconfirmed (the decompile-derived "bit 4 = 0" reading is contradicted by the capture; see the 67ac8801 characteristic's `status_byte` field): an already-enrolled lock answers RegisterAdmin with error 05, which is the reliable signal.

rejoin.notes: Additional users are enrolled in place: the new client obtains the admin's current password out-of-band (the official app sends it by SMS — there is no server), sends UserRegistrationRequest (0x90) carrying that password plus its bytewise complement, then UserRegistration (0x91) to install its own admin ID and time-based password. RemoveUser (0x81) revokes a user. A factory reset is only needed when all credentials are lost.

testing.notes: Static analysis of the official Android app (UUIDs, opcodes, frame layout, checksum and name patterns re-checked against a second read, 2026-08) PLUS one over-the-air capture of the vendor app driving a unit (2026-08-30). The capture confirms bonding enforcement, the command frame and checksum, and the enrollment/factory-password/ GetMac exchanges — but the vendor app crashed before ever sending TimeStamp/OpenLock, so unlock itself is unobserved, and nothing here has been replayed from this spec by a third-party client yet. Status-byte polarity and the battery scale remain open.

variants.model: BS1609 TouchLock TSA BT (TSA luggage lock)
OEM rebadges speaking the same protocol (e.g. locks advertising Joi_Lock)

entities.name: Unlock
entities.notes: Momentary: the protocol has an OpenLock command but no Lock command (the lock re-engages itself), so this is a press, not a toggle. Requires the unlock_password credential; the vendor flow syncs the lock RTC (TimeStamp 0x01) before opening — whether the lock insists on that ordering is part of the pending hardware check.

entities.name: Lock State
entities.notes: Bit 7 of the `status_byte` field on the notify characteristic (multiplexed frames: use only frames whose `opcode` field is 0xff). Polarity UNCONFIRMED — which value means locked is part of the pending hardware check; bit-level extraction is not expressible in the characteristic's `format`, so a consumer decodes per the `status_byte` field's notes.

entities.name: Battery
entities.notes: Bits 2..0 of the `status_byte` field (0xff frames only), as a RAW 0-7 level — the percentage mapping is unverified (n/7 is the candidate), and an observed 3 -> 1 drop within one session means the field may not be a plain battery gauge. Same bit-extraction caveat as Lock State. The same byte is broadcast in advertisement manufacturer data, so a passive listener can track it without connecting.

artifacts.description: Static analysis of the OEM Android app for this lock family (2026-08). Source of every byte-level fact in this spec: the GATT UUIDs and write type from its scan/connect layer, the 20-byte frame layout, opcodes and checksum from its command builder, the advertised-name patterns from its name matcher, the time-derived password and status-byte layout from its crypto helper, and the response codes from its error enum. Its settings screen is also where the absence of any upgrade/OTA path was confirmed.
artifacts.obtained_via: third-party APK mirror, 2026-08 (the Play listing was gone; no official download)

artifacts.artifact: Android HCI snoop (bugreport btsnoop_hci.log) of the vendor app driving one padlock unit, 2026-08-30, ~15 minute session
artifacts.description: First over-the-air capture for this family. Confirms: bonding is enforced (an SMP security request precedes all GATT traffic; legacy Just Works, lock IO NoInputNoOutput, full LTK/IRK/CSRK distribution); the 20-byte command frame and 0x5A-seed checksum (the RegisterAdmin frame verifies, and its time-derived password bytes equal the session's wall-clock time); RegisterAdmin (0x80), ChangeFactoryPassword (0x8c/0x8d) and GetMac (0xad) dispatched with success responses; an unsolicited UpdateStatus (0xff) notification at ~1 Hz for the whole connection; the GATT handle map (notify 0x000e, CCCD 0x000f, write 0x0011). Also shows the vendor app crashing before ever sending TimeStamp/OpenLock — unlock remains unverified on hardware — and a status-byte sequence (0x13 -> 0x03 -> 0x01) that contradicts the decompile-derived 'bit 4 = registered' reading.
artifacts.obtained_via: owner's phone, 2026-08; the log stays uncommitted — it contains the owner's identifiers and credentials, only derived facts appear here

covers: unlock (TimeStamp 0x01 then OpenLock 0x00) over local BLE with no cloud
admin and user enrollment/revocation (0x80/0x90/0x91/0x81), factory reset (0x8f)
passive lock-state + battery tracking from the manufacturer-data status byte in advertisements, without connecting
not_covered: firmware update — no OTA mechanism exists in the app or (apparently) the product
remote access — the product has no network interface at all; any remote control means a local BLE bridge (e.g. an ESPHome bluetooth_proxy host) within radio range

change_factory_password_data.advanced_reason: Changes the password that gates factory reset. If the new value is lost and admin credentials are also lost, no software recovery path is known. Record the new password before sending.
change_factory_password_data.description: Second half of changing the factory password. Payload A: old factory password. Payload B: new factory password. Observed in the capture with a success response.
change_factory_password_data.name: ChangeFactoryInitPasswordData

change_factory_password_request.description: First half of changing the factory password. Payload A: admin ID. Payload B: admin ID again. Observed in the capture with a success response.
change_factory_password_request.name: ChangeFactoryPasswordRequest

factory_init.advanced_reason: Wipes every enrolled credential on the lock; all clients must re-enroll afterwards. Mistyping the factory password just returns error 03, but a successful reset on a lock you cannot physically reach to re-enroll leaves it unusable remotely.
factory_init.description: Factory reset over BLE. Payload A: admin ID. Payload B: the 8-character factory password, one hex-digit character per byte (the app dialog hints the default is 00000000). Clears admin and all users; the lock returns to the unregistered state.
factory_init.name: FactoryInit

find_lock.description: Locate the lock (presumably audible/visual on the device — modality unconfirmed). Payloads are a fixed pattern: A = 22 44 66 88 88 66 44 22, B = 11 33 55 77 77 55 33 11.
find_lock.name: FindLock

get_mac.description: Observed in the capture (the app dispatches it right after RegisterAdmin): the reply echoes opcode ad with error 00 and carries the requesting CENTRAL's own BD_ADDR byte-reversed in the frame body — not the lock's address, despite the name.
get_mac.name: GetMac

get_user_info.description: Defined in the app's command builder but never dispatched by its UI — response layout unknown.
get_user_info.name: GetUserInfo

open_lock.description: Unlock. Payload A: the stored 8-byte unlock password. Payload B: the new time-based password, which becomes the stored password on success. The app always sends TimeStamp (0x01) first and retries once with the previous password on error 03.
open_lock.name: OpenLock

register_admin.description: Enroll the first/primary admin on an unregistered lock. Payload A: 8-byte admin ID (client-generated, time-derived in the app). Payload B: the new time-based password. Observed in the capture with a success response; its password bytes equal the session's wall-clock time.
register_admin.name: RegisterAdmin

remove_user.description: Revoke an enrolled user. Payload A: admin ID. Payload B: the 8-byte user ID to remove.
remove_user.name: RemoveUser

time_stamp.description: Sync the lock RTC: bytes 2-7 carry yy MM dd HH mm ss, each decimal field written as one hex-parsed byte; bytes 8-17 are zero. Must succeed before OpenLock in the app flow; whether the lock tolerates large clock skew is unknown.
time_stamp.name: TimeStamp

update_status.description: Header of the lock's unsolicited status notification (not a command the client sends). Pushed about once per second for the entire connection once notifications are enabled — observed throughout the capture.
update_status.name: UpdateStatus

user_registration.description: Second half of user enrollment. Payload A: admin ID. Payload B: the new user's time-based password.
user_registration.name: UserRegistration

user_registration_request.description: First half of enrolling an additional user. Payload A: the current 8-byte admin password. Payload B: bytewise complement (XOR 0xFF) of payload A.
user_registration_request.name: UserRegistrationRequest

crypto.enrollment_ids: The admin ID is also time-derived: eight two-digit groups from the current time, joined with colons. A local client may use any 8-byte value; only uniqueness per lock matters (error 05 on re-registration).
crypto.rolling_password: The 'time-based password' is the current timestamp formatted yy-MM-dd-HH-mm-ss-SSSS, split into eight two-digit decimal groups, each group written as one byte parsed as hexadecimal. Example: 26-08-18-19-05-23-84-62 becomes bytes 0x26 0x08 0x18 0x19 0x05 0x23 0x84 0x62. Capture-confirmed: the RegisterAdmin frame's password bytes equal the capture session's wall-clock time to the second. On a successful OpenLock the new time-based password carried in payload B becomes the stored password; the previous one is kept as a one-shot fallback (retried once on error 03, then the app aborts). The scheme is trivially predictable by anyone who has observed one exchange and knows the approximate time — treat BLE bonding as the only real (and weak) barrier, and note this spec exists precisely so owners are not locked out by it.

framing.byte_order: big-endian (single-byte fields; no multi-byte integers in any command)
framing.checksum: byte[19] = (0x5A - sum(bytes[0..18])) & 0xFF — additive checksum with a 0x5A seed, confirmed in the app's checksum helper AND verified against the capture (a RegisterAdmin frame's checksum byte reproduces exactly). The same computation is applied to every command frame regardless of opcode.
framing.notes: Fixed 20-byte command frame: [0] opcode, [1] 0x00, [2..9] payload A (8 bytes), [10..17] payload B (8 bytes), [18] 0x00, [19] checksum. Multi-byte 'values' such as the admin ID travel as eight independent bytes (colon-joined hex strings in the app), so endianness never arises. A separate 14-byte peripheral-command writer taking (adminId[0..5], 00 00, 6-byte arg) exists in the app's command builder but has NO callers — dead code or factory-use, recorded so nobody chases it.

remaining_unknowns: Bluetooth SIG company ID of the manufacturer-data advertisement and the exact AD layout around the status byte (the 2026-08-30 capture contains no advertising reports)

Status-byte polarity (bit 7: 1 = locked or unlocked?), the battery 0-7 to percentage mapping, and the meaning of the observed 0x13 -> 0x03 -> 0x01 transitions that contradict the decompile's 'bit 4 = registered' reading
Response-frame checksum rule: observed responses fit chk = (0x5A - sum(bytes[0..2])) & 0xFF with byte 3 excluded — confirm whether byte 3 is a flag outside the checksum or the rule differs
GetUserInfo (0x82) response layout (never dispatched in the app UI or the capture)
Whether OEM siblings (Joi_Lock etc.) run identical firmware — likely (same app) but never captured
Lock RTC tolerance to clock skew (TimeStamp must succeed before unlock)
A caller-less 14-byte peripheral-write command — dead code or factory-use
Whether 67ac8800 is advertised in scan responses or only visible after connection
Whether the lock accepts OpenLock payload B equal to payload A (no rotation); the vendor flow always rotates

responses.layout: 5-byte frames on the notify characteristic: [0] echoed opcode, [1] error code, [2] status byte, [3] frame flag (00 or 01 in the capture), [4] checksum. The checksum does NOT follow the command rule verbatim: every observed response fits chk = (0x5A - sum(bytes[0..2])) & 0xFF, i.e. byte 3 is excluded — treat that as observed behaviour to re-check, not as proven layout.
responses.verification_note: Frame layout, error echo and the GetMac special case all observed in the 2026-08-30 capture: the GetMac (0xad) reply carries the requesting central's own BD_ADDR byte-reversed. GetUserInfo (0x82) was never dispatched; its response layout is still unknown.

session_flow.description: Unlock session as implemented by the app's connection and main screens: scan -> connect -> bond -> discover services -> enable notifications on 67ac8801 (then a ~1.2 s pause). If the lock is unregistered, send RegisterAdmin (0x80). To open: send TimeStamp (0x01) to sync the lock RTC — success here is required before the app will proceed — then OpenLock (0x00) carrying the stored password in payload A and the new time-based password in payload B. On success the new password replaces the stored one. An optional app-level PIN (default 33333333) or phone fingerprint gates the unlock button — phone-side UI only, NOT part of the BLE protocol. NOTE: in the 2026-08-30 capture the vendor app crashed after changing the factory password and never reached the TimeStamp/OpenLock exchange, so it remains unobserved on the wire.
session_flow.verification_note: Reconstructed from the vendor app's command dispatch; the unlock half has never been observed on the wire (the captured session crashed before it).

characteristics.description: Notify. Every observed frame is 5 bytes: [0] echoed opcode, [1] error code, [2] status byte, [3] small flag/counter (00 or 01 in the capture), [4] checksum. Error codes: 00 success, 01 invalid command, 02 checksum error, 03 incorrect password, 04 invalid user ID, 05 already registered, 06 user record full, 07 unbonded device. Two frame families share this characteristic: command responses (echoed opcode) and the unsolicited UpdateStatus (opcode ff), which the lock pushes about once per second for the entire connection once notifications are enabled. Enable via CCCD 0x2902 immediately after service discovery.

format.name: status_byte
format.notes: Bit layout from the decompile: bit 7 lock state, bit 4 registered flag, bits 2..0 battery level 0-7. The capture PARTIALLY CONTRADICTS this: the observed sequence was 0x13 (session start, lock already enrolled) -> 0x03 (immediately after a successful RegisterAdmin — bit 4 CLEARED by registration, the opposite of the app's own reading) -> 0x01 (later in the same session). Treat bit 7 = lock state (polarity still unconfirmed) and bits 2..0 = battery 0-7 as the working model, and the bit 4 claim as disputed. The observed low bits changed 3 -> 1 within minutes, which is a fast drop for a battery — possibly a real discharge event, possibly not a plain battery field. One controlled lock/unlock + vendor-app battery reading will settle all three.

format.name: frame_flag
format.notes: 00 or 01 in the capture; excluded from the response checksum — see protocol_details.command_protocol.responses.

characteristics.name: Command response / status (lock -> client)

factory_init.advanced_reason: Wipes every enrolled credential on the lock; all clients must re-enroll afterwards. Mistyping the factory password just returns error 03, but a successful reset on a lock you cannot physically reach to re-enroll leaves it unusable remotely.
factory_init.description: Factory reset over BLE. Payload A: admin ID. Payload B: the 8-character factory password, one hex-digit character per byte (default hinted as 00000000 -> eight 0x00 bytes). Clears admin and all users; every client must re-enroll afterwards.

admin_id.description: The 8-byte admin ID enrolled on the lock.

factory_password.description: The 8-character factory password, one hex-digit character per byte (default hinted as 00000000 -> eight 0x00 bytes).

find_lock.description: Locate the lock (presumably audible/visual on the device — modality unconfirmed). Fixed payload pattern; the trailing checksum byte 0xC6 is the frame rule applied to the pattern.

open_lock.description: Unlock. Payload A: the stored 8-byte unlock password. Payload B: the password that replaces it on success — the vendor app rotates it to a fresh time-derived value every unlock (see protocol_details.command_protocol.crypto); binding it to the SAME credential here means no rotation, which the pending hardware check must confirm the lock accepts. The vendor flow sends TimeStamp (0x01) first and retries once with the previous password on error 03.

checksum.notes: (0x5A - sum(bytes[0..18])) & 0xFF — a subtract-from-seed, NOT the sum+XOR idiom `auto: checksum` encodes.

new_password.description: The password that becomes stored on success. Bound to the same credential as stored_password (no rotation) until time-derived rotation is implemented.

stored_password.description: The lock's current 8-byte unlock password, raw bytes. Installed at enrollment and rotated by every successful unlock in the vendor flow. If the vendor app was used before, this is whatever password it last rotated to — the vendor flow's fallback is the previous one.

register_admin.description: Enroll the primary admin on an unregistered lock (error 05 if one is already enrolled). Payload A: the 8-byte admin ID the CLIENT invents. Payload B: the first password. Both must be stored locally — there is no recovery path but factory reset.

admin_id.description: The 8-byte admin ID this client uses on the lock. Any value works (the vendor app derives it from the current time); only uniqueness per lock matters.

admin_password.description: The admin's initial 8-byte password (the vendor flow uses the current time-derived password).

characteristics.description: Write-without-response (Write Command, handle 0x0011). Every command is exactly 20 bytes: [0] opcode, [1] 0x00, [2..9] payload A, [10..17] payload B, [18] 0x00, [19] checksum = (0x5A - sum(bytes[0..18])) & 0xFF — capture-verified on a RegisterAdmin frame. See `protocol_details.command_protocol.commands` for the full opcode table; the `commands` below are the subset rendered as controls. TimeStamp (0x01) is NOT among them: its payload is the current wall-clock time, which the declarative template cannot express — see protocol_details for its layout.
characteristics.name: Command write (client -> lock)

services.description:
The only application GATT service. 20-byte command frames are written to the write characteristic; responses and unsolicited status arrive on the notify characteristic. The app's scan screen also defines a service-filter constant for 00001801 (Generic Attribute), but the actual scan is unfiltered (empty ScanFilter, batch mode) — 0x1801 is not known to be on the lock and is not listed as a service here. The standard Battery Service (0x180F / 0x2A19) appears in the bundled Nordic BLE library but is apparently unused by the app flow — battery comes from the status byte instead.
Handle map from the capture: notify characteristic value at 0x000e (its CCCD at 0x000f), write characteristic value at 0x0011; the whole GATT database spans handles 0x0001-0x0024. The default MTU of 23 suffices — the 20-byte frame is exactly one ATT write, which is why the frame is 20 bytes.
services.name: TouchLock lock service
